title: Frankenstein
author: Mary Shelley
openingChapterLabel: Letter I — Walton to his Sister
openingText: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings. I arrived here yesterday, and my first task is to assure my dear sister of my welfare and increasing confidence in the success of my undertaking.
about:
Victor Frankenstein, a student from Geneva, discovers how to give life to lifeless matter. Horrified by the being he creates, he abandons him. The creature learns language and observes human affection from a hiding place beside a family’s cottage, but his attempts to find companionship meet with rejection. By the time he asks Victor to create a companion for him, he has already killed Victor’s younger brother and framed an innocent woman. Their conflict draws both creator and creature into a pursuit that ends in the Arctic.

First published in 1818, Frankenstein was revised by Mary Shelley in 1831; this edition follows the later text. Its story reaches us through several narrators. The explorer Robert Walton writes to his sister, records Victor’s account, and within it passes on the creature’s own story. Each voice asks for understanding, and each gives the reader reasons to question it.

The novel combines horror, speculative science, family tragedy, and a debate about responsibility. It asks what a creator owes a being capable of suffering, how exclusion can shape a life, and whether suffering can ever excuse violence.

angleCards.title: Hearing the creature
angleCards.text: The creature describes how he learned to care for people and then turned against them. I want to weigh his account without overlooking his victims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Frankenstein to consider the creature’s account of rejection and revenge, asking where explanation ends and justification begins.

angleCards.title: A creator’s responsibility
angleCards.text: Victor gives life to a being and immediately abandons him. I want to follow how he understands his obligations and how those obligations conflict.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Frankenstein to examine Victor’s responsibilities toward his creature and other people, especially when he considers making a companion.

angleCards.title: Ambition and its limits
angleCards.text: Walton and Victor both seek exceptional achievements. I want to compare what each risks and how each responds when other lives are endangered.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Frankenstein to compare Walton’s and Victor’s ambitions and ask what makes someone stop a dangerous pursuit.

angleCards.title: Who tells the story?
angleCards.text: Walton records Victor, and Victor recounts the creature’s words. I want to notice how these voices guide my sympathy and where their perspectives differ.
angleCards.angleObjective: I’m reading Frankenstein to follow its nested narrators, asking how framing, omissions, and self-defence affect what I believe.

cast.name: Victor Frankenstein
cast.description: A student from Geneva whose fascination with natural philosophy leads him to discover how to animate lifeless matter. He abandons the being he creates. His account alternates between self-reproach, blame, and attempts to justify his decisions.

cast.name: The Creature
cast.description: An unnamed being, eight feet tall, who learns language by observing the De Lacey household. His reading includes Paradise Lost, Plutarch’s Lives, and The Sorrows of Young Werther. He longs for affection, commits murder, and asks his creator for a companion.

cast.name: Robert Walton
cast.description: An English explorer seeking a northern passage. He takes the exhausted Victor aboard his ship and records his story in letters to his sister Margaret. His own expedition raises questions about ambition and responsibility toward others.

cast.name: Elizabeth Lavenza
cast.description: In this revised version, Elizabeth is an Italian orphan taken into the Frankenstein family. She grows up with Victor and later becomes his wife. Her letters show her concern for those around her, including the accused Justine.

cast.name: Henry Clerval
cast.description: Victor’s childhood friend, interested in literature and languages. He nurses Victor in Ingolstadt and later travels with him through England and Scotland. They separate before Victor goes to work alone on an Orkney island.

cast.name: The De Lacey Family
cast.description: A French family living in exile: the blind father, his son Felix, and his daughter Agatha. Safie joins them, and the creature learns by listening to her lessons. When he approaches the father, Felix attacks him, Agatha faints, and Safie flees.

whyItMatters.title: Responsibility after creation
whyItMatters.body: Victor’s achievement begins a relationship he is unwilling to face. The creature’s demands make responsibility an ongoing problem: care for him may conflict with duties to other people. The novel gives both the abandonment and the later violence moral weight.

whyItMatters.title: Sympathy without easy absolution
whyItMatters.body: The creature’s story makes his suffering intelligible without undoing the deaths he causes. Victor also describes genuine grief while defending choices the reader may question. Reading their accounts together means holding sympathy and judgment in tension.

whyItMatters.title: Knowing when to stop
whyItMatters.body: Walton hears Victor’s story while his own crew faces death in the ice. Victor’s ambition therefore becomes more than a distant warning: another person must decide what to do in a related crisis. The ending leaves us comparing their words with their actions.
